required_facts.statement: Problem framing clarifies the problem rather than choosing a solution.
Write a concise problem statement identifying who is affected, what the problem is, why it matters, and where it occurs.
State what work is included and what is excluded to make the scope boundary explicit.

text.content: Imagine an operations manager saying, “We need a new order system.” That names a possible solution, but it leaves the underlying problem unclear. For this example, suppose dispatch staff at the North branch cannot find the latest delivery instructions, and repeated clarification calls delay dispatch. Those details let you frame a problem without deciding what to buy.

text.title: Problem Definition and Scoping
text.content: Problem framing clarifies the problem rather than choosing a solution.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Write a concise problem statement identifying who is affected, what the problem is, why it matters, and where it occurs. State what work is included and what is excluded to make the scope boundary explicit.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
A bounded statement could read: “North-branch dispatch staff cannot reliably find the latest delivery instructions when preparing an order, causing repeated clarification calls and delayed dispatch.” It identifies who is affected, what is wrong, why it matters, and where it occurs. The sentence does not promise that a new system is the right response.

Now write the boundary beside it: “Included: finding and communicating the latest delivery instructions during North-branch dispatch preparation. Excluded: changing delivery prices, replacing vehicles, or changing other branches' operations.” These are invented boundaries for this exercise, not general exclusions for every BA assignment. If a stakeholder asks to redesign vehicle purchasing, compare that request with the stated included and excluded work. The useful output is a problem statement and an explicit boundary, not a list of features disguised as a problem.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: “Implement an app” is not the same as clarifying the problem. Reword it around the affected people and difficulty before deciding on a solution. A concise problem statement also does not replace the included and excluded work: both need to be visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the operations manager's complaint, “We need a new order system,” into one paragraph using the supplied North-branch dispatch situation. Identify who is affected, what the difficulty is, why it matters, and where it occurs, then explicitly state included and excluded work.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted paragraph identifies North-branch dispatch staff, difficulty finding the latest delivery instructions, repeated clarification calls and delayed dispatch, and the North-branch dispatch preparation setting. It explicitly includes finding and communicating the latest delivery instructions and excludes changing delivery prices, replacing vehicles, and changing other branches' operations, without committing to a solution.

visual_anchor.purpose: Place the vague complaint beside the bounded North-branch problem statement. Annotate who, what, why, and where, and display the included and excluded work separately so the distinction between a proposed solution, a defined problem, and its scope boundary is visible.

notes: Keep solution requirements and document templates for later; establish the problem and boundary first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

text.content: Suppose dispatch staff describe delivery instructions as “hard to use.” You need to learn what happens during preparation, not persuade them that a particular replacement is desirable. Set the interview aim as understanding the expected outcome, current operating conditions, and constraints on accessing instructions.

text.title: Structured Interviews
text.content: A structured interview follows an interview script, unlike a semistructured interview’s flexibly ordered guide.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Define what needs to be learned and prepare questions that address those aims. Ask concise, open-ended questions that let the participant describe their experience without suggesting the answer. Record the elicited needs in a shared requirements document with links to the supporting interview context. Probe vague answers with follow-up questions about concrete expected outcomes, operating conditions and constraints, and observable or measurable criteria showing that the requirement has been met.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Prepare a script with questions such as “Describe how you find the instructions for an order,” “What information do you need before dispatch?” and “What happens when that information is unclear?” A structured interview follows that script; a flexibly ordered guide would instead be semistructured. Keep each question concise and leave room for the participant’s own account.

When a participant says, “It should be quick,” ask what concrete outcome they expect, under which conditions, and what observable or measurable result would show that the need is met. For this hypothetical interview, they might specify finding the current instructions within 30 seconds during dispatch preparation. Record that elicited need in the shared requirements document and link it to the interview context, including the conditions discussed. The numerical threshold is example stakeholder input, not a universal requirement. The finished record should preserve both the stated need and the context that supports it, rather than only your summary of “make it faster.”

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Open-ended does not mean directionless: the questions still serve defined learning aims. Conversely, asking “Would a new mobile screen fix this?” suggests an answer instead of letting the participant describe their experience. A vague answer calls for concrete follow-up, not an invented requirement.

practice_anchor.objective: Conduct a mock structured interview with one person playing a dispatch staff member who finds delivery instructions hard to use. Define learning aims, prepare and follow an interview script, use concise open-ended questions, and probe vague answers. Produce a list of elicited requirement statements in a shared requirements document, linking each statement to supporting interview context.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted script and interview record show questions aligned with defined learning aims, a scripted sequence, and nonleading wording. Follow-up questions establish concrete expected outcomes, operating conditions, constraints, and observable or measurable signs that each elicited need is met. Requirement statements preserve the persona's answers and link to the relevant interview context; any numerical thresholds come from the mock participant rather than being assumed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the dispatch example's progression visible: a defined learning aim, a concise scripted question, the vague answer 'It should be quick,' concrete follow-up questions, and a recorded requirement linked to its interview context. Annotate the hypothetical 30-second threshold as stakeholder input, not a universal rule.

notes: Do not turn this into workshop facilitation or survey design; teach script, open questions, probing, and contextual recording first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A workshop uses goal-oriented group activities and discussion to produce shared outcomes.
Build the agenda by defining goals, identifying questions needed to reach them, and choosing activities that answer those questions.
Allocate time to each workshop segment and prepare the materials needed to capture discussion.
Guide discussion toward the agenda goals and analyze and share the collected outputs after the workshop.

text.content: Imagine dispatch, sales, and customer-support representatives disagreeing about which delivery instructions must be available before dispatch. A workshop brings them together for goal-oriented activities and discussion. Define its outcome as a shared account of the information needed, with any unresolved questions recorded.

text.title: Facilitated Workshops
text.content: A workshop uses goal-oriented group activities and discussion to produce shared outcomes.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Build the agenda by defining goals, identifying questions needed to reach them, and choosing activities that answer those questions. Allocate time to each workshop segment and prepare the materials needed to capture discussion. Guide discussion toward the agenda goals and analyze and share the collected outputs after the workshop.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Build the agenda from that goal. Questions might include “What must dispatch know?” and “Which team supplies each piece of information?” Choose activities that address those questions, such as having participants describe an order and then discuss the required information together. In this hypothetical agenda, allocate ten minutes to the goal, twenty to the order exercise, twenty to discussion, and ten to consolidating outputs. Prepare a shared capture sheet before the session so contributed requirements and questions have a place to go.

During discussion, guide contributions back to the agenda’s questions. A lengthy discussion of vehicle purchasing does not answer the agreed information question, so return to the intended outcome. Afterward, analyze the captured material and share the resulting requirements and unresolved questions with participants. The workshop is not finished merely because its time has elapsed: the collected outputs still need analysis and sharing. The example timings and activity are choices for this situation, not a mandatory workshop format.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A workshop is not simply several people receiving the same presentation. Its activities and discussion are directed at shared outcomes. A detailed agenda helps only when its questions and activities actually support the agreed goals.

practice_anchor.objective: Design and run a 90-minute requirements workshop with a small group representing dispatch, sales, and customer support. Define the shared information outcome, identify the questions needed to reach it, choose activities that answer those questions, allocate all 90 minutes, and prepare a shared capture sheet. Guide discussion toward the goals, then analyze and share the resulting requirements and unresolved questions.
practice_anchor.success: Submit the agenda, completed capture sheet, and shared post-session summary. The agenda connects goals to questions and activities, with segment timings totaling 90 minutes. The captured outputs and a brief facilitation record demonstrate that discussion stayed directed toward the information needed before dispatch. The summary distinguishes shared requirements from unresolved questions and records that it was shared with participants.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible a 90-minute agenda linking each segment's goal, question, activity, duration, and capture materials, alongside a completed capture sheet showing the delivery information requirements and unresolved questions contributed by dispatch, sales, and customer support.

notes: Keep named workshop methodologies short; avoid implying one mandatory agenda sequence.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Surveys are best suited to collecting quantitative attitudinal data rather than detailed accounts of behavior.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that Respondents Can’t Answer Accurately

required_facts.statement: Include questions needed to answer the research aims rather than collecting information simply because it is easy to ask for.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that You Can Find the Answer to

required_facts.statement: Write questions that respondents can answer accurately and avoid language that leads them toward a preferred answer.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that Respondents Can’t Answer Accurately; Avoid Biasing Respondents

text.content: Suppose an order-service team wants to understand preferences across several branches. The research aim is to compare how important respondents consider finding delivery instructions quickly. A survey fits that attitudinal question better than a request for a detailed account of everything someone actually does during dispatch.

text.title: Surveys and Questionnaires
text.content: Surveys are best suited to collecting quantitative attitudinal data rather than detailed accounts of behavior.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Include questions needed to answer the research aims rather than collecting information simply because it is easy to ask for. Write questions that respondents can answer accurately and avoid language that leads them toward a preferred answer.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
An example question could be “How important is access to the latest delivery instructions when preparing dispatch?” with clearly stated response options. Another could ask how satisfied the respondent is with current access. Keep questions tied to the stated research aim. Asking about unrelated office preferences would collect information without answering the requirements question.

Compare “How satisfied are you with the current instruction lookup?” with “How much do you love our improved lookup?” The second pushes toward a favorable answer. Also check whether respondents can accurately answer what is being asked: a person who does not prepare dispatch may not be able to describe that experience. In this exercise, the survey’s output is quantified attitudes and preferences about instruction access. It is not a reconstruction of the actual sequence of dispatch work. Maintain that distinction when explaining the results to stakeholders so the requirements discussion does not treat a preference score as a detailed behavioral account.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A large set of responses does not change the kind of evidence collected. Stated attitudes remain attitudes; they are not detailed observations of behavior. Easy-to-ask questions also do not belong automatically: each should serve the research aims.

practice_anchor.objective: Draft a 10-question stakeholder requirements survey for the hypothetical order-service team, focused on attitudes and preferences about finding delivery instructions quickly across branches. Justify each question by explaining its connection to the research aim, why the intended respondents can answer it accurately, and how its wording avoids suggesting a preferred answer.
practice_anchor.success: A submitted survey contains 10 relevant questions with clearly stated response options. Each question has a justification linking it to the research aim and explaining its answerability and neutral wording. The survey collects attitudes and preferences about instruction access without claiming to reconstruct actual dispatch behavior.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the contrast between neutral and leading question wording visible using the instruction-lookup example. Annotate the preferred wording for relevance to the research aim and respondent answerability, and distinguish quantified attitudes from detailed accounts of dispatch behavior.

notes: Do not introduce sampling statistics or claim surveys directly establish actual behavior.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Existing documentation is one channel for gathering requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels

required_facts.statement: Extract the requirements, assumptions, constraints, and open questions found in existing material and record them in one shared document with links to supporting context.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels; Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Confirm the documented requirements with stakeholders before treating them as execution work.

text.content: Imagine being given an old dispatch manual and a contract for an order-service change. The manual says a supervisor approves amended delivery instructions; the contract says the service must retain an instruction record. These are example statements from existing material, not requirements you have independently confirmed.

text.title: Document Analysis
text.content: Existing documentation is one channel for gathering requirements.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Extract the requirements, assumptions, constraints, and open questions found in existing material and record them in one shared document with links to supporting context. Confirm the documented requirements with stakeholders before treating them as execution work.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Review the material systematically and record what each statement contributes. Put the approval requirement and record-retention constraint in the shared requirements document, linking each to the supporting manual or contract passage. If the manual assumes that only one branch processes an order, record that assumption too. If the contract does not identify who may amend instructions, record an open question rather than filling the gap with your own preference.

Then confirm the documented requirements with the relevant stakeholders before treating them as work to execute. For example, ask whether the supervisor approval rule is still intended and which scope it covers. A stakeholder might confirm it, request a change, or leave a question unresolved; preserve the resulting understanding in the shared record. The practical skill is extracting requirements, assumptions, constraints, and questions with their context intact. Merely copying paragraphs into a new file leaves the learner without a clear account of what has been found and what still needs confirmation.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Existing text is an elicitation channel, not automatic confirmation that every old statement should be implemented now. Keep the supporting context and confirm requirements with stakeholders; do not silently turn an unresolved passage into an agreed requirement.

practice_anchor.objective: Review invented dispatch-manual and order-service document passages. Extract explicit and implied requirements into one shared record, distinguish assumptions, constraints, and open questions, and link each entry to its supporting passage.
practice_anchor.success: The shared record captures the supervisor approval requirement, instruction-record retention constraint, single-branch assumption, and unresolved authority to amend instructions. Any implied requirement is identified as an inference rather than an agreed requirement. Each entry links to supporting context, and requirements are marked as needing stakeholder confirmation before execution.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the extraction visible in an annotated table pairing invented source passages with the extracted requirement, assumption, constraint, or open question, a supporting-context link, and a stakeholder-confirmation status.

notes: Avoid contractual or regulatory interpretation; use invented document statements only.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Observation examines what users do in their work context rather than relying solely on their account of what they do.
Watch the user perform work, then ask questions about what was observed.
Record the tasks performed and analyze their sequence and subtasks to understand how the goal is achieved.
Record the user’s stated process, compare it with the steps observed during actual work, and log discrepancies with notes of the observed actions that support them.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ — When to Use Contextual Inquiry; The 4 Phases of Contextual Inquiry — 1. The primer, 3. The contextual interview, 4. The wrapup

text.content: Suppose a dispatcher says, “I open the order and send it to the driver.” Observe the dispatcher doing the work in its actual context, then ask about the actions you saw. In this example, you observe the dispatcher open the order, consult a separate instruction sheet, call sales to clarify an address, and then send the order to the driver.

text.title: Observation Techniques
text.content: Observation examines what users do in their work context rather than relying solely on their account of what they do.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Observe the user perform work, then ask questions about what was observed. Record the tasks performed and analyze their sequence and subtasks to understand how the goal is achieved. Record the user’s stated process, compare it with the steps observed during actual work, and log discrepancies with notes of the observed actions that support them.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Record the performed tasks and their sequence. You can describe the goal as preparing an order for dispatch and identify subtasks such as finding instructions and resolving uncertainty. Ask questions about those observed steps: “What information were you checking on the separate sheet?” or “What made the clarification call necessary?” These questions follow the observation instead of replacing it with a guessed explanation.

Keep the stated process alongside the observed process. The statement omitted the separate-sheet lookup and clarification call; log that discrepancy with notes of the observed actions that support it. Do not change the observation record to make the two accounts agree. The comparison helps you understand how this work was actually performed in the observed situation. It does not establish that every dispatcher always follows the same sequence. The useful result is a supported account of tasks and discrepancies that can inform requirements, not a judgment about whether the participant gave a good interview answer.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Observation is more than asking someone what they normally do. It examines work as performed and then uses questions to understand what was seen. A difference between an account and observed steps should be documented with action notes, not replaced by speculation about motive.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a dispatcher task walkthrough alongside the dispatcher's stated process. Record the observed tasks, their sequence and subtasks, log discrepancies with supporting action notes, and identify follow-up questions about the observed actions.
practice_anchor.success: The record distinguishes the stated steps of opening and sending the order from the observed sequence of opening the order, consulting a separate instruction sheet, calling sales to clarify an address, and sending the order. It identifies the omitted lookup and clarification call with supporting action notes and includes follow-up questions grounded in those actions rather than guessed motives.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the dispatcher's stated process alongside the observed task sequence, with the separate-sheet lookup and clarification call marked as omitted from the stated account and supported by action notes.

notes: Keep process notation for later; teach task records and stated-versus-observed comparison.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Distinguish validation of the intended business need with stakeholders from verification of the written requirements’ quality: stakeholder agreement does not by itself establish that the wording is unambiguous or objectively testable.

required_facts.statement: Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, requirement categories, assumptions, and constraints; record missing information as open questions for resolution.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Check ambiguity by asking whether stakeholders can interpret the statement the same way; replace vague wording with plain, outcome-focused language and measurable thresholds where possible.

required_facts.statement: Check testability by identifying an executable test and an objective pass/fail result for each stated condition; revise a condition if its satisfaction depends on subjective judgment.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/acceptance-criteria — Characteristics of good acceptance criteria — Testability; How to write acceptance criteria — 3. Establish overall testability

text.content: Imagine stakeholders agreeing that dispatch staff need “a fast instruction lookup.” Agreement confirms an intended need, but the wording still leaves several questions: what counts as fast, under what conditions, and how will anyone determine whether the requirement has been met?

text.title: Requirements Validation and Verification
text.content: Validation with stakeholders confirms priorities and agreement about what will be delivered.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: For the requirements review, present the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions, then capture stakeholder agreement or requested changes. Distinguish validation of the intended business need with stakeholders from verification of the written requirements’ quality: stakeholder agreement does not by itself establish that the wording is unambiguous or objectively testable. Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, requirement categories, assumptions, and constraints; record missing information as open questions for resolution. Check ambiguity by asking whether stakeholders can interpret the statement the same way; replace vague wording with plain, outcome-focused language and measurable thresholds where possible. Check testability by identifying an executable test and an objective pass/fail result for each stated condition; revise a condition if its satisfaction depends on subjective judgment.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Present the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions to stakeholders, capturing agreement or requested changes. That addresses validation of the intended business need. Separately verify the written requirement. Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, categories, assumptions, and constraints. If the operating conditions are missing, record an open question rather than assuming them.

For ambiguity, ask whether stakeholders interpret “fast” the same way. In this hypothetical case, they clarify the requirement as “During normal dispatch preparation, the current instructions for a selected order are displayed within two seconds.” The condition and threshold are example decisions made by these stakeholders. For testability, identify an executable test: select an order in the stated conditions, measure the time until its current instructions appear, and compare that time with two seconds. The pass/fail result is objective; “it felt fast” is not.

The review therefore has two different outputs: agreement about the intended need, and wording that has been checked for completeness, ambiguity, and testability. Keep unresolved questions visible until the missing information is resolved.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Approval does not by itself prove that a sentence is unambiguous or testable. Nor does a precise threshold prove the requirement serves the intended business need. Validation and verification address different questions, so one cannot stand in for the other.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a flawed requirements list for dispatch instruction lookup alongside the documented goal, scope, stakeholder priorities, success metrics, assumptions, and constraints. Classify each defect as a validation or verification issue, then correct it using the supplied information. Record unresolved information as open questions rather than inventing decisions.
practice_anchor.success: Requirements that address the wrong need are identified as validation issues and corrected to reflect the supplied stakeholder decisions. Missing information, vague wording, and subjective conditions are identified as verification issues. Revised requirements use plain, outcome-focused wording and supported measurable thresholds, with an executable test and objective pass/fail result for each stated condition. Any correction needing further stakeholder agreement is recorded as a requested change.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an annotated dispatch requirements list beside the documented business need. Contrast a precisely worded requirement serving the wrong need with a relevant requirement containing vague wording, then show their classifications, supported corrections, and any unresolved questions.

notes: Keep the validation/verification distinction explicit; do not invent mandatory test tooling.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A low-fidelity prototype is an inexpensive, relatively simple representation used to explore and test a design.
Sketch a wireframe by drawing the screen’s main content areas and controls without detailed visual styling.
Use a prototype to gather feedback about a design before investing in a fully implemented version.

text.content: Suppose stakeholders struggle to explain what they need on a delivery-instruction screen. Instead of implementing the screen, draw a simple representation for discussion. A low-fidelity prototype can be inexpensive and relatively simple while still letting stakeholders explore a design.

text.title: Prototyping and Wireframing for Requirements Elicitation
text.content: A low-fidelity prototype is an inexpensive, relatively simple representation used to explore and test a design.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Sketch a wireframe by drawing the screen’s main content areas and controls without detailed visual styling. Use a prototype to gather feedback about a design before investing in a fully implemented version.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this example, sketch a page with an order identifier at the top, a large area for current instructions, and controls labeled “Select order” and “Confirm instructions.” These labels and areas are invented design choices for the exercise. Leave out detailed colors, typography, and visual styling. The wireframe’s job here is to represent the main content areas and controls, not to establish the final appearance.

Use the sketch to gather feedback before investing in a fully implemented version. A dispatcher might point to the instruction area and ask for the last amendment to be visible; another might explain that the confirmation control does not match their intended task. Record what the feedback reveals rather than treating every drawn control as an agreed requirement. The representation gives stakeholders something concrete to respond to while the design is still being explored. After discussion, the useful output is feedback about the design and needs it surfaces, not a claim that the screen is complete simply because all its boxes have labels.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A wireframe need not look like a finished interface. Adding detailed styling is not what makes this low-fidelity elicitation useful. Also distinguish the proposed design from the feedback collected about it: a sketched control is not automatically an agreed requirement.

practice_anchor.objective: Sketch a low-fidelity delivery-instruction screen with an order identifier, a current-instructions area, and controls labeled Select order and Confirm instructions. Use simple shapes and labels without detailed styling. Given a dispatcher’s request to see the last amendment and their statement that confirmation does not match the intended task, list the new need and the correction or clarification to pursue.
practice_anchor.success: The sketch clearly represents the main content areas and controls without finished styling. The learner records the need to make the last amendment visible and identifies the confirmation control as needing clarification or revision, without inventing an agreed replacement. The proposed design remains distinct from requirements revealed through feedback before implementation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a low-fidelity delivery-instruction wireframe visible, with labeled content areas and controls and annotations linking stakeholder reactions to the newly revealed need and the control requiring clarification.

A circle marked L stands for the logo, and boxes represent menu entries, with shading indicating the current selection. A large banner area includes arrows and dots to represent controls for moving between images. Below it, a crossed box marks an image location, a title area indicates a heading, and lines stand for description text. Labels identify the menu, banner, and about-us section so someone else can understand the sketch. These website elements are example choices, not requirements for every screen.

Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Brainstorming generates alternative ideas for a shared problem.
State the session’s problem and goal, set a time limit, choose a facilitator, and record contributed ideas.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-collaboration/brainstorming/how-to-run-a-brainstorming-session — Step 1. Identify your goal; Step 3. Set a time and place; Step 4. Pick a qualified facilitator

required_facts.statement: Keep idea generation separate from judging ideas so participants can explore possibilities.

text.content: Imagine the team has agreed on the problem “Dispatch staff cannot find current delivery instructions.” The brainstorming goal is to generate alternative ideas for addressing that problem, not to decide immediately which idea wins.

text.title: Brainstorming
text.content: Brainstorming generates alternative ideas for a shared problem.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: State the session’s problem and goal, set a time limit, choose a facilitator, and record contributed ideas. Keep idea generation separate from judging ideas so participants can explore possibilities.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
State the problem and goal to the participants. For this hypothetical session, choose a facilitator, set a fifteen-minute limit, and prepare a place to record ideas. Contributors suggest a single instruction summary, a clearer amendment label, or a revised handoff between sales and dispatch. Record those contributed ideas so the discussion does not depend on remembering who said what.

Keep generation separate from judgment. If a participant responds to the first suggestion with “That will never work,” the facilitator can return the session to generating alternatives and leave evaluation for a separate discussion. This does not mean every idea must later be selected. It means the current activity is exploration, so an idea is recorded before it is judged.

At the end, the result is a set of alternatives connected to the same shared problem. The example ideas are possibilities, not recommended solutions. The distinction matters for a BA: a session aimed at generating ideas should not be described as if it had already established requirements or chosen an implementation. The facilitator, limit, and record provide a concrete frame for that exploration.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Separating generation from judgment is not the same as promising to implement every suggestion. Brainstorming produces alternatives for a shared problem. A session that immediately debates each contribution is mixing the two activities rather than preserving the stated separation.

practice_anchor.objective: Run a timed brainstorming session on the hypothetical problem “Dispatch staff cannot find current delivery instructions.” State the goal of generating alternatives, choose a facilitator, set a fifteen-minute limit, and capture every contributed idea without filtering.
practice_anchor.success: The session has an explicit shared problem, a generation goal, a facilitator, and a time limit. The raw record preserves all contributed ideas, including those challenged by participants. The facilitator redirects judgment to a separate discussion, and the session ends with a broad set of alternatives rather than a selected solution.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a hypothetical session board with the dispatch problem, the generation goal, a named facilitator, a fifteen-minute limit, and an unfiltered idea list containing a single instruction summary, a clearer amendment label, and a revised sales-to-dispatch handoff. An annotation makes clear that judgment is deferred and the listed alternatives are not selected solutions.

text.content: Suppose an order-service team wants to hear how dispatch staff feel about a proposed instruction summary. A focus group is a moderated discussion of attitudes and opinions. Prepare a moderator script around specific issues: whether the summary feels clear, which information participants consider important, and where their preferences differ.

text.title: Focus Groups
text.content: A focus group is a moderated discussion that gathers participants’ attitudes and opinions.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Prepare a moderator script with specific issues and goals for the information to be gathered. Keep discussion on topic, invite all participants to contribute, and prevent one participant from dominating. Record the opinions and disagreements expressed in the discussion without treating those stated preferences as evidence of actual product use.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
In the hypothetical discussion, one participant says the latest amendment should be most prominent; another prefers the complete instruction history. Record both opinions and the disagreement. Invite quieter participants to contribute and keep the conversation on the script’s issues. If one participant takes over, guide the discussion so their view does not become the only view captured.

The resulting record might say, “Participants disagreed about showing a summary versus a complete history,” with the preferences they expressed. It should not say, “Dispatchers use summaries during actual work,” because that behavior was not established by this discussion. The group’s stated preferences can inform requirements exploration without being relabeled as observation.

For the BA, the practical output is a supported account of attitudes, including disagreement. The moderator’s script keeps the information goal visible, while balanced participation lets more than one perspective be expressed. The invented design choices in this example are prompts for discussion, not a finding that either choice is the correct solution.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A focus group does not become evidence of actual product use merely because participants describe what they prefer. Keep stated opinions and disagreements as such. Moderating participation also does not require erasing disagreement to make the record look unanimous.

practice_anchor.objective: Draft a moderator guide for a hypothetical order-service team's focus group about a proposed instruction summary for dispatch staff.
practice_anchor.success: The guide states the information goals, includes prompts about clarity, important information, and differing preferences, and provides moderator wording to return to the topic, invite quieter participants, and redirect a dominant speaker. It includes a recording section that preserves both agreement and disagreement as expressed opinions without presenting them as evidence of actual product use.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible a hypothetical discussion record showing participant preferences for the latest amendment or complete instruction history, areas of agreement and disagreement, and an explicit distinction between stated preferences and actual use that has not been established.

media.group_title: Focus groups: gathering opinions and balancing participation

segments.label: How moderator prompts elicit attitudes and opinions
segments.summary: A focus group brings together participants recruited against research objectives. The explanation describes groups of six to ten people, sometimes recruited through agencies offering rewards. A moderator prompts participants to share product opinions or emotional reactions to advertising. Indirect prompts, such as imagining brands as animals, can help participants express feelings that direct questions might not uncover.

segments.label: Redirecting a dominant speaker and inviting quieter participants
segments.summary: During a discussion of airline inconveniences, one participant gives an extended baggage account that drifts into train travel. The moderator acknowledges the contribution and redirects the discussion to another participant. A second example shows the moderator inviting a quieter participant to contribute and asking her to elaborate. The explanation also encourages exchanges between participants when they begin engaging with one another. These interventions create space for more voices rather than allowing one account to occupy the discussion.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the first clip uses moderator prompts to elicit feelings, then how the second redirects a lengthy contribution and invites quieter voices. Their recruitment and airline examples are illustrations, not universal rules.
bridge_note.after: The first clip covers attitudes; the second covers participation. Neither teaches script preparation or separating preferences from actual use. The text fills those gaps and supplies the definition and moderation guidance each clip does not teach.
